In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Sharh

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ ﴿And We relieved you of your burden﴾ ﴿which had weighed down your back﴾ ﴿And We raised high your remembrance﴾

Here Allah mentions three matters: the expansion of the breast (sharh al-sadr), the removal of the burden (wada' al-wizr), and the raising of remembrance (raf' al-dhikr).

Although they are introduced by an interrogative, it is a rhetorical interrogative (istifham taqriri) used to establish an affirmation. So His saying ﴿Did We not expand﴾ means "We have expanded," according to the well-known principle that the negation of a negation is an affirmation. This is because the interrogative hamza, which carries the sense of negation, entered upon lam, which is for negation, so the two cancelled each other out and the verb remained affirmative. They said: similar to it is His saying ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ [al-Zumar: 36], and His saying ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 18].

Upon this is the saying of the poet:

"Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts,
and the most generous of all the worlds in the bellies of wine?"

Thus it is established that Allah enumerates upon him His great blessings. We have mentioned earlier the connection of this surah with the one before it, in completing the blessings of Allah upon His Messenger (ﷺ).

Al-Nisaburi narrated from 'Ata' and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz that they used to say: this surah and Surah al-Duha are one surah, and they used to recite them in a single rak'ah, and they did not separate between them with the basmala. What prompted them to this is that His saying ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ is like a continuation (ʿatf) of His saying ﴿Did He not find you an orphan?﴾ [al-Duha: 6]. This claim, namely that they are one surah, was rejected. In any case, even if this does not make them one surah, it makes them linked together in meaning, as with al-Anfal and al-Tawbah.

[p. 573]

The meaning of the expansion of the breast has been differed about, but there is no contradiction in what they said, and each complements the others.

It was said: it is the splitting of the breast, whether once or more, and its washing and filling with faith and wisdom, as in the narration of Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah concerning the night of the Isra', and the narration of Abu Hurayrah concerning other occasions.

In it, as in the narration of Ahmad: "His breast was split open, and rancour and envy were removed from it, in something like a clot of blood, and compassion and mercy were inserted into it."

It was said: the expansion of the breast is only its widening for knowledge, faith and recognition of the truth, and making his heart a vessel for wisdom.

In al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Allah expanded his breast for Islam."

According to Abu Kathir: We illuminated it and made it spacious, roomy and wide, like His saying ﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast for Islam﴾ [al-An'am: 125].

What the Qur'an bears witness to is that sharh is inshirah (openness) and irtiyah (gladness). This is a state resulting from the firm establishment of faith, knowledge, light and wisdom, as in His saying ﴿Is one whom Allah has expanded his breast for Islam, so he is upon light from his Lord?﴾ [al-Zumar: 22]. So His saying ﴿so he is upon light from his Lord﴾ explains the expansion of the breast for Islam.

Just as the constriction of the breast is a sign of misguidance, as in the same verse: ﴿And whoever Allah wills to misguide, He makes his breast constricted and tight﴾, to the end of the verse [al-An'am: 125].

In the margin of Shaykh Zadah 'Ali on al-Baydawi, he said: Allah did not expand the breast of anyone of the worlds as He expanded his breast, peace be upon him, until it encompassed the knowledge of the earlier and the later ones, so he said: "I have been given comprehensive words (jawami' al-kalim)." End of quotation.

What he means by the knowledge of the earlier and the later ones is what came in the Qur'an of the reports of past nations with their messengers, and the reports of the Return, and what lies between that, of what Allah taught him.

What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that the expansion of the breast by which he (ﷺ) was favoured is broader and more general than that, to the extent that it includes his patience, his forgiveness, his pardoning of his enemies, and his repaying evil with good, to the point that it embraces the enemy just as it embraces the friend.

Like the story of his return from Ta'if, when its foolish people harmed him, until the angel of the mountains was distressed by their conduct, and Jibril said to him: "Indeed the angel of the mountains is with me; if you wish, he will close the two mountains upon them, and he will do so." His breast expanded beyond that, and it was as though they had not wronged him, so he said: "O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know. Indeed I hope that Allah will bring forth from their loins one who will say: There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah."

That is the greatest blessing and the strongest aid in conveying the call and bearing the burdens of the message. For this reason Allah's prophet Musa turned to his Lord asking for it, when he was commanded to go to the tyrant Pharaoh, as in His saying ﴿Go to Pharaoh, indeed he has transgressed﴾ ﴿He said: My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾ ﴿and ease for me my task﴾ ﴿and untie the knot from my tongue﴾ ﴿that they may understand my speech﴾ ﴿and appoint for me a minister from my family﴾ ﴿Harun, my brother﴾ ﴿strengthen through him my back﴾ [Ta-Ha: 24-31].

Here he mentioned four factors of help in performing the message. He began with the expansion of the breast, then the easing of the task; these two are intrinsic factors. Then the means between him and Pharaoh, which is the tongue in persuasion: ﴿untie the knot from my tongue﴾ ﴿that they may understand my speech﴾. Then finally the material factor of support: ﴿appoint for me a minister from my family﴾ ﴿Harun, my brother﴾ ﴿strengthen through him my back﴾. He placed the expansion of the breast before all of this because of its importance, for by it one confronts all difficulties. Therefore he confronted with it the great magic brought by the sorcerers, and the greater severity Pharaoh threatened them with.

Allah has explained, among the causes of the expansion of the breast and its illumination, what comes from elevation, wisdom and facilitation. Some of this category is aided by receiving those teachings from revelation, such as His saying ﴿Take what is easy of forgiveness, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], and His saying ﴿those who restrain anger and pardon people, and Allah loves the good-doers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134], which is achieved only by one whose breast Allah has expanded. Among what helps one to persevere in it is the expansion of the breast. Indeed he (ﷺ) endured the harm of the polytheists in Makkah and the deception of the hypocrites in Madinah, and received all of that with a spacious breast.

In this, as we have mentioned, there is direction for every caller to Allah: that he should have a spacious breast, a calm soul, and be adorned with patience.

His saying ﴿And We relieved you of your burden﴾ [al-Nur: 2]. Wada' (laying down) is used for reducing and lightening, and it is also used for loading and making heavy. If it is followed by 'an, it means reducing; if followed by 'ala, it means loading, as in their saying: "I put down from you" (wada'tu 'anka) and "I put upon you" (wada'tu 'alayka). Wizr linguistically means weight.

From this root: ﴿until the war lays down its burdens﴾, meaning its weight of weapons and the like.

From it also: the wazir (vizier), who bears the weight and preoccupation of his ruler. In the Shari'ah it means sin, as in the hadith: "Whoever establishes an evil practice, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection." The two terms may alternate in expression, as in His saying ﴿that they may bear their burdens in full﴾ [al-Nahl: 25], and His saying in another place ﴿and they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13].

The word wizr is mentioned here in the singular and unrestricted, and it is not specified what it is or what kind it is, so scholars have differed greatly about it.

It was said: it is what was in him of the affairs of the jahiliyyah, and his being protected from sharing in them, so nothing of it reached him.

It was said: it is the weight of his distress at what his people were upon, and his inability to change it, along with his compassion for them (ﷺ). This is like His saying ﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief over their footsteps if they do not believe in this message﴾ [al-Kahf: 6], i.e., out of grief over them.

Abu Hayyan said: it is a metaphor for his immunity (ʿismah) from sins and his purification from defilements.

Ibn Jarir said: "And We forgave you what preceded of your sins, and We removed from you the weight of the days of ignorance in which you were."

Ibn Kathir said: it means that Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what followed.

So the words of Abu Hayyan indicate immunity, the words of Ibn Jarir indicate something of the jahiliyyah, and the words of Ibn Kathir are general.

In this domain is the topic of the infallibility (ʿismah) of the prophets in general, a question of usul (principles of jurisprudence) which the books of usul investigate for the soundness of the call. The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and him, has previously discussed it in Surah Ta-Ha at His saying ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121], presenting the views of the Mu'tazilah, the Shi'ah and the Hashwiyyah, and the criterion for that, rationally and legally. And in Surah Sad at His saying ﴿And David thought that We had tested him, so he asked forgiveness of his Lord﴾ [Sad: 24], where he alerted that everything said about David, peace be upon him, concerning this meaning consists entirely of Isra'iliyyat which do not befit the station of prophethood. End of quotation.

As for him specifically (ﷺ), we present the following. Whatever the case, his immunity (ʿismah) from major and minor sins after the mission (ba'thah) must be affirmed with certainty, due to the explicit text of the Noble Qur'an in His saying ﴿Indeed you have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21], since following him is obligatory, and it is impossible that anything of that should be in him, definitively.

As for before the mission, immunity from major sins must also be affirmed with certainty, because he (ﷺ) was in a state of preparation for prophethood from his youth. His breast was split in the age of nursing, and the portion of Satan was removed from it. Moreover, had anything occurred from him, they would have seized upon it when they opposed his call, and nothing of that is mentioned. So nothing remains except the discussion of minor sins, and these are between permissibility and prohibition. If they were permissible and occurred, they do not touch his station (ﷺ), because they occurred before the mission and the obligation, and they were forgiven and their weight was removed from him. And if they did not occur and were not permissible for him, then this is what is sought.

Al-Alusi, may Allah have mercy on him, related in his tafsir that his uncle Abu Talib said to his brother al-'Abbas one day: "I have held him close to me, and I have not separated from him night or day, and I have not entrusted him to anyone." He mentioned the story of his sleeping among his sons at the beginning of the night, and then his transferring him to the place of one of his sons to protect him. Then he said: "I never saw from him a lie, nor laughter, nor any jahiliyyah, nor did he stop with the children while they played."

The books of tafsir mention that he (ﷺ) once, in his youth, wished to go to a wedding place to see what was there, but when he drew near it, sleep overcame him and he did not awaken except by the heat of the sun. So Allah protected him from seeing or hearing anything of that.

From it is also the story of his participation in building the Ka'bah, when he was stripped and was immediately prevented from it. On the prevention of anything occurring from him (ﷺ), the answer regarding the meaning of the verse remains. It is said, and Allah knows best, that it is an honouring of him (ﷺ), as in the case of the people of Badr, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr" and said: "Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you," although they would not do anything forbidden thereby. It is an honouring of them and a raising of their rank.

[p. 577]

He (ﷺ) used to repent, seek forgiveness, and stand in prayer at night until his feet swelled, and he said: "Shall I not be a grateful servant?"

So all of that from him was thankfulness to Allah, the Exalted, and a raising of his ranks (ﷺ).

It has come: "What a fine servant Suhayb is; had he not feared Allah, he would not have disobeyed Him," and that is one of the good deeds of his (ﷺ).

Or he (ﷺ) used to count against himself any shortcoming, and regard as a sin something he found burdensome, and he would seek forgiveness from it, just as when he came out of the privy he would say: "Ghufranak" (I seek Your forgiveness).

It is known that there is no cause that makes seeking forgiveness obligatory, except what is said: that his awareness of omitting remembrance (dhikr) in that state required that of him.

The scholars have approved the saying of al-Junayd: "The good deeds of the righteous are the misdeeds of those brought near (to Allah)." Or the meaning is like what came in the Qur'an about some of his (ﷺ) *ijtihad* (independent judgment, personal effort at reasoning) in the course of calling to the religion. His *ijtihad* is then corrected, and this weighs heavily on him, as in the story of Ibn Umm Maktum, for which he was rebuked: ﴿He frowned and turned away, because the blind man came to him﴾ [Abasa: 1-2], and its like, even if it came after the revelation of this surah. Yet it belongs to the same category as His saying: ﴿Allah pardon you! Why did you give them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43], the story of the captives of Badr, His saying: ﴿You have no part in the affair﴾ [Al 'Imran: 128], and his *ijtihad* regarding the faith of his uncle, until it was said to him: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas: 56], and similar things. So the verse is understood in this light. Or the *wizr* (burden) is in its linguistic meaning, namely what weighed upon him of the burdens of the call and the conveying of the message, as Ibn Kathir mentioned in the commentary on Surat al-Isra' from Imam Ahmad, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When it was the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I awoke in Makkah and was distressed, and I knew that the people would deny me. So I sat apart, grieving. Abu Jahl passed by me, came and sat down beside me, and said to me, as one mocking: 'Has anything happened?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Yes,' and he related the Night Journey to him."

In it is the explicit statement that he (ﷺ) was distressed, and distress is a heaviness and grief, and grief is a heaviness. The expectation of their denial weighed on the soul more than anything else. And Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who weighed down your back﴾, that is, its heaviness, indicates that sin has a heaviness upon the believer by which he is bowed down, and nothing lightens it except repentance and its removal in His sight.

His saying: ﴿And We raised high your mention﴾ does not specify here by what or how He raised his mention. Raising can be sensory (*hissi*) or immaterial (*ma'nawi*), so the intended meaning has also been disputed.

It has been said: it is sensory, in the call to prayer (*adhan*) and the summons to standing prayer (*iqamah*), in sermons on the pulpits, and in the openings of speeches on important matters. They argued for this from what actually occurs, and they cited the words of Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him, from a rhyming-in-*dal* qasida in his Diwan:

*An illustrious (sign) upon it is a seal for prophethood,*
*from Allah, witnessed, shining and bearing witness.*
*And Allah joined the name of the Prophet to His own name,*
*when the muezzin says in the five (prayers): "I bear witness."*
*And He split for Him from His name, to exalt him:*
*the Lord of the Throne is Mahmud, and this is Muhammad.*

And from raising the mention in meaning, that is, from exaltation, is his (ﷺ) being mentioned in the books of the prophets before him, so that he was known to the earlier nations before his coming.

The Qur'an has explicitly stated that Allah made the revelation a remembrance for him and his people, in His saying: ﴿So hold fast to what has been revealed to you; indeed, you are upon a straight path﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 43-44]. It is known that his people's being mentioned is a mention of him, as the poet said:

*How many a father has risen through a son to heights of rank,*
*just as 'Adnan was exalted through the Messenger of Allah.*

Thus it becomes clear that the raising of his mention (ﷺ) is only through the path of revelation, whether by explicit texts addressing him, such as: ﴿O Messenger﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41], ﴿O Prophet﴾ [al-Anfal: 64], ﴿O you wrapped in garments﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1], and the explicit naming of his name in the station of prophethood: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Fath: 29]; or in the branches of legislation, as was mentioned before, in the call to prayer, the summons to standing prayer, the tashahhud, sermons, and prayer upon him (ﷺ). And Allah knows best.

**Verse 94:7** "So when you are free, then labour [in worship]," and **verse 94:8** "and to your Lord direct your longing."

Al-nasab (exertion) is fatigue after striving, as in His words: ﴿Faces that Day will be humbled, labouring and weary﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 2-3].

Exertion may be for this world or for the Hereafter, and the verse does not specify what the exertion is for, so the scholars differed. Their opinions are close in meaning.

It was said: it refers to the supplication after finishing the prayer.

It was said: it refers to voluntary prayers beyond the obligatory ones. What the Qur'an supports, however, is that it is a general directive to take up the share of the Hereafter after finishing the work of this world, as in His words: ﴿And during part of the night, pray with it as an additional [prayer] for you; it is expected that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [al-Isra': 79], and His words: ﴿Indeed, the rising at night is more effective for concentration and more suitable for words﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 6], meaning that it is the time when the day's work is finished and the night is quiet; and His words: ﴿When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest, and you see the people entering into the religion of Allah in multitudes, then exalt [Allah] with the praise of your Lord and ask His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance﴾ [al-Nasr: 1-3].

Thus a person's whole time is occupied, either with this world or with religion.

In His words ﴿So when you are free, then labour﴾ there is a solution to the problem of "free time" which has preoccupied the world, since it leaves the Muslim no free time in his life: he is either engaged in work for this world or in work for the Hereafter.

It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he passed by two men wrestling, and said to them: "We were not commanded this after our free time."

It is also narrated from 'Umar that he said: "I truly dislike for any one of you to be idle and aimless, neither in the work of this world nor in the work of religion." For this reason, the earliest generation did not regard free time within the day as a problem.

Among what points to the state of the earliest generation is what Malik narrated from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, who said: "I said to 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, while I was then a young man: 'Have you considered the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever makes pilgrimage to the House or visits [it in 'umrah], there is no blame upon him for walking between them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158]? So is there anything upon a man in not walking between them?' 'Aishah said: 'No; if it were as you say, it would have read: "There is no blame upon him for not walking between them."'"

Consider, may Allah have mercy on you and me, what a young man thinks about, and how he raises difficulties regarding the meanings of the Qur'an. Someone like him does not have free time.

**Note.**

Al-Alusi mentioned, regarding His words "fa-nsab," an irregular recitation (shadhdh) with a kasra on the ṣād (fa-nsib). The Shi'ah took it to mean: when the Prophet is free from prophethood, appoint 'Ali as imam. He said: the matter is not necessarily restricted to 'Ali; a Sunni can say: "fa-nsab Abu Bakr." If the Shi'i argues with what happened at Ghadir Khumm, the Sunni argues that that time was not the time of the Prophet's being free from prophethood.

Indeed, his ﷺ saying, "Order Abu Bakr to lead the people in prayer," was after it, near the time of his ﷺ being free from prophethood, since it was during his final illness in which he died.

If the Shi'i argues from the freeing from the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajj al-Wada'), the Sunni refuses by saying that the verse came before that. End of quotation.

In any case, if the Shi'ah argue with it, it suffices to refute their argument that it is an irregular recitation. Pursuing irregular recitations is close to the kind of distorted interpretation (ta'wil) called al-la'b by the scholars of tafsir, which is turning a word away from its apparent meaning without any indicating context or connecting link.

Among the distorted interpretations of this verse is what some common people do. I saw an ordinary commoner wearing a complete outfit: a turban, a smooth garment and a fine belt, of what they call a nasbah, meaning a complete suit. Someone said to him: "What is this nasbah, so-and-so?" He replied: "When I finish my work, I dress up (nasabt), as Allah said: ﴿So when you are free, then labour﴾."

I also heard another complaining about how little he had, saying to his companion: "Don't you know someone I can nasb upon?" meaning: someone from whom I can take a loan. I said to him: "Why would you nasb upon him? Nasb is lying and forbidden." He said: "If a person has nothing, and his hand is empty, there is no harm; because Allah said: ﴿So when you are free, then labour﴾." Such things, and their like, are what the common people venture into because of their ignorance, or what people of desires do because of their sects.
